questions: Does the "minimum path of length k" refer to the smallest possible sum of cell values visited, the smallest number of steps, or some other metric?
Is the starting cell counted as part of the path length k, i.e., does a path of length k contain k cells or k moves?
May cells be revisited multiple times within the same path, or must each cell be visited at most once?
Are diagonal neighbor moves allowed, or only the four orthogonal (up, down, left, right) moves?
Must the path stay entirely within the grid boundaries, or are wrap‑around moves (toroidal topology) permitted?
If multiple paths achieve the same minimum metric, should any particular tie‑breaking rule be applied (e.g., lexicographically smallest sequence of coordinates)?
Are there any constraints on the values of k relative to N (e.g., k ≤ N*N), or can k be larger than the number of distinct cells?
Should the function return the minimum metric value, the actual sequence of coordinates, or both?
answers: The lexicographically smallest sequence of the values on the visited cells (comparing position by position), not a sum or step count.
A path of length k means visiting exactly k CELLS (not k moves).
Yes, cells CAN be revisited; they are not required to be distinct.
No, only the four orthogonal (up/down/left/right) neighbor moves that share an edge are allowed.
No, the path must stay entirely within the grid boundaries; going off the grid is not allowed.
The answer is guaranteed to be unique per the specification, so no additional tie-breaking rule is needed beyond the lexicographic comparison.
Not addressed beyond k being a positive integer; since cells can be revisited, k is not bounded by N*N.
The actual ordered sequence of the VALUES on the visited cells, not just the metric and not the coordinates themselves.
